datasets.name: e-SNLI
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in the few-shot common-NLP-task study with PaLM-540B; evaluated by accuracy. The paper’s default is the test split when labels are available.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in the few-shot common-NLP-task study with PaLM-540B; evaluated by accuracy. The paper’s default is the test split when labels are available.

baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same model and prompts as self-consistency; the paper specifies 8 manually written arithmetic exemplars and 4–7 randomly selected training exemplars for each commonsense task.

baselines.name: Sample-and-rank
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on GPT-3 code-davinci-001 using the same number of sampled sequences as self-consistency; selects the final answer from the highest-log-probability sequence.

baselines.name: Beam search decoding (top beam)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on UL2-20B under the same number of beams and reasoning paths.

baselines.name: Ensemble with 40 prompt-order permutations
baselines.fair_comparison: Greedy decoding with exemplars randomly permuted 40 times, with answers combined by majority vote.

baselines.name: Ensemble with 3 prompt sets
baselines.fair_comparison: Greedy decoding with 3 manually written prompt sets, with answers combined by majority vote.

metrics.name: Consistency (% of decodes agreeing with the final aggregated answer)

controls.name: CoT-prompting with greedy decoding
controls.detail: The same model and prompt setup without self-consistency’s multiple sampled reasoning paths and answer aggregation.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unmodified decoding reference for judging whether the self-consistency condition improves performance.

confounds.name: Gains come from generating multiple candidates or extra inference, rather than answer consistency
confounds.detail: Self-consistency samples many outputs, so improvement might be attributable merely to using multiple generations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with sample-and-rank on GPT-3 code-davinci-001 using the same number of sampled sequences; sample-and-rank improves accuracy less.

confounds.name: Gains depend on a particular sampling strategy or parameter choice
confounds.detail: The reported gains could be specific to the temperature, top-k, or nucleus-sampling settings used in the main experiments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Vary temperature, top-k, and nucleus-sampling p on PaLM-540B and report that self-consistency is robust across strategies and parameters.

confounds.name: Gains are an effect of prompt choice or prompt-order sensitivity
confounds.detail: Prompt sets or the order of exemplars could themselves account for apparent improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against greedy-decoding ensembles using 3 manually written prompt sets and 40 prompt-order permutations; both yield smaller gains than self-consistency.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated runs and reported variability
evidence_standards.detail: Main results average 10 runs, sampling 40 outputs independently per run. Results are reported with standard deviations where shown; the paper omits standard deviations for Table 2 because they are at most 0.5, and plots accuracy means and standard deviations over 10 runs. No statistical test or numerical significance threshold is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Sampling and decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: For UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B, temperature 0.5 with top-k 40; for PaLM-540B, temperature 0.7 with top-k 40; for GPT-3, temperature 0.7 without top-k truncation.

datasets.name: PrOntoQA
datasets.eval_protocol: No train/validation/test split is specified. Uses 8-shot in-context prompts and greedy decoding. Evaluates 1-, 3-, and 5-hop examples with top-down or bottom-up ontology sentence ordering and fictional, true, or false ontologies; runs 400 generated examples per experiment combination (48 experiments). Parses predicted CoT sentences into logical forms and scores labels and reconstructed proofs.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on PrOntoQA under the same 8-shot, greedy-decoding setup and task-variable settings as the other model checkpoints.

metrics.name: label accuracy
metrics.caveat: A correct label may be guessed through heuristics and does not establish that the model reasoned correctly; the paper also analyzes predicted CoTs using proof-accuracy metrics.

metrics.name: strict proof accuracy
metrics.caveat: Requires canonical proof steps and may underestimate reasoning ability; the paper also reports more permissive proof-accuracy metrics.

metrics.name: valid proof accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper's proof-correctness definition allows a correct proof to contain invalid steps, provided there is a path of allowed proof steps from premises to conclusion.

metrics.name: first non-canonical step type in incorrect proofs
steps taken after a misleading step before returning to the gold proof

confounds.name: Pretraining knowledge or retrieval, rather than reasoning, explains success
confounds.detail: Real-world concepts may let the model retrieve facts or skip proof steps, making performance look like reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares fictional and false ontologies with true ontologies. The paper reports that the model can reason above chance on fictional examples, while also finding much better performance on true ontologies, indicating that pretraining knowledge helps.

confounds.name: Spurious correlations or shortcuts allow the model to guess answers without reasoning
confounds.detail: A model could exploit correlations in examples to predict the answer without following the proof.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says it adds distractor sentences to remove shortcuts that would allow guessing the answer; the provided text does not specify further measurements.

confounds.name: Correct answers arise without correct reasoning
confounds.detail: Label accuracy alone could be high because the model guesses the label or uses a heuristic, even when its CoT does not establish the answer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Parses predicted CoTs into logical forms and compares label accuracy with several proof-accuracy measures; reports that label accuracy is poorly correlated with strict proof accuracy.

evidence_standards.name: 95% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Computes 95% confidence intervals for each experiment using the Wilson method, treating the number of correct proofs as binomial.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding
evidence_standards.detail: Main experiments are reported with greedy decoding.

datasets.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
datasets.eval_protocol: 23 BIG-Bench tasks (27 subtasks); three few-shot exemplars per task. A random subset of 250 evaluation examples is used for all but Causal Judgement, Penguins in a Table, and Snarks, for which all available test examples are used (187, 146, and 178, respectively), in addition to the three few-shot examples. Total: 6,511 evaluation examples. Prompts include task instructions and answer options; CoT prompts use manually composed CoT exemplars. Greedy decoding (temperature 0); final answers are extracted using expected keywords and scored by exact match.

baselines.name: Answer-only few-shot prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with CoT prompting using the same evaluation setup, including task instructions and answer options; the paper describes the answer-only approach as few-shot prompting without CoT.

metrics.name: Exact-match accuracy
metrics.caveat: For multiple-choice tasks, this differs from rank/scoring classification, which scores options individually by likelihood; the paper instead supplies all options together, generates an answer, and measures exact match.

metrics.name: Average and maximum human-rater performance
metrics.caveat: The authors caution that human-rater scores may not represent human performance reliably: task formatting and content changed, raters had limited time, and they could use external resources. They warn that exceeding average human-rater performance should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning.

metrics.name: Unweighted average accuracy across BBH tasks

controls.name: Answer-only prompting
controls.detail: Few-shot prompting without CoT, run alongside CoT prompting; both setups include task instructions and answer options.
controls.rules_out: That CoT results are explained merely by including task instructions and answer options; the comparison measures the difference associated with adding CoT prompting to this setup.

confounds.name: Human-rater baseline scores may not represent reliable human performance
confounds.detail: A model exceeding the average human-rater score could reflect limitations in the human comparison rather than human-level language understanding or reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper reports average and maximum human-rater scores but explicitly cautions that task changes, limited rater time, and access to external resources make the scores hard to interpret.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding
evidence_standards.detail: All language-model results are reported with temperature set to 0. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: AIME24
datasets.eval_protocol: All 30 problems; accuracy (pass@1), with temperature 0 (greedy) unless otherwise specified. Figures needed by some problems are provided as Asymptote vector graphics. Test-time scaling evaluations vary thinking-token compute; data-ablation scores use budget forcing with a maximum of around 30,000 thinking tokens.

datasets.name: MATH500
datasets.eval_protocol: The same 500 samples selected by OpenAI in prior work; accuracy (pass@1), with temperature 0 (greedy) unless otherwise specified.

datasets.name: GPQA Diamond
datasets.eval_protocol: The Diamond subset only (198 PhD-level science questions); accuracy (pass@1), with temperature 0 (greedy) unless otherwise specified.

baselines.name: Token-conditional control (TCC)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on AIME24 using s1-32B; the methods are evaluated across varying test-time compute.

baselines.name: Step-conditional control (SCC)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on AIME24 using s1-32B; the methods are evaluated across varying test-time compute.

baselines.name: Class-conditional control (CCC)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on AIME24 using s1-32B; the methods are evaluated across varying test-time compute.

baselines.name: Rejection sampling
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on AIME24 using s1-32B; rejection sampling uses temperature 1 and samples until generations fit specified thinking-token budgets.

baselines.name: Majority voting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as parallel test-time scaling; for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, 64 evaluations per sample at temperature 1 are used to examine voting across different numbers of generations.

baselines.name: REBASE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other scaling approaches on AIME24 using 16 parallel trajectories; the paper notes REBASE’s extra reward-model forward-pass compute.

baselines.name: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking Experimental
baselines.fair_comparison: The authors benchmark it themselves on AIME24 by manually entering all 30 questions in the web interface; they omit MATH500 and GPQA Diamond because of API recitation errors.

metrics.name: Accuracy (pass@1)
metrics.caveat: Accuracy alone does not describe whether a method controls test-time compute or improves as compute increases; the paper also reports Control and Scaling for test-time scaling methods.

controls.name: s1-32B without budget forcing
controls.detail: The finetuned model is evaluated without the test-time budget-forcing intervention.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported gain over the base model requires budget forcing at test time.

controls.name: 1K-random
controls.detail: Select 1,000 high-quality reasoning chains at random, without the difficulty or diversity filtering.
controls.rules_out: Whether the curated-data result is explained simply by using 1,000 high-quality examples.

controls.name: 1K-diverse
controls.detail: Select 1,000 examples uniformly across domains, without selecting for difficulty.
controls.rules_out: Whether diversity alone accounts for the curated-data result.

controls.name: 1K-longest
controls.detail: Select the 1,000 examples with the longest reasoning traces.
controls.rules_out: Whether selecting long traces as a difficulty proxy alone accounts for the curated-data result.

controls.name: 59K-full
controls.detail: Train on the full 59K-example pool instead of the selected 1K examples.
controls.rules_out: Whether using more training examples, rather than the paper’s 1K selection, accounts for the result.

controls.name: No extrapolation
controls.detail: Evaluate without repeatedly suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter and appending a continuation string.
controls.rules_out: Whether the extrapolation results reflect repeated budget-forcing interventions rather than the unextended condition.

controls.name: 2x without string
controls.detail: Suppress the end-of-thinking delimiter twice without appending a continuation string.
controls.rules_out: Whether the effect of repeated budget forcing is due merely to continuing without the delimiter, rather than the appended string.

confounds.name: Evaluation-question contamination in the training data
confounds.detail: Training examples overlapping with evaluation questions could inflate benchmark performance without reflecting general reasoning ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors decontaminate the data against MATH500, GPQA Diamond, and AIME24 using 8-grams and deduplicate the data.

confounds.name: Parallel sampling, rather than sequential test-time scaling, explains the performance gains
confounds.detail: The apparent benefit of using more test-time compute could come from generating multiple independent solutions and voting, rather than from sequential refinement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare against majority voting on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and report that scaling the base model with majority voting does not catch up with s1-32B.

evidence_standards.name: Paired bootstrap uncertainty for data ablations
evidence_standards.detail: For differences relative to s1K, report 95% paired bootstrap confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap samples.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation-run counts for test-time scaling comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Table 3 reports the number of evaluation runs used to estimate method properties: 5 for BF, TCC, TCC + BF, SCC, SCC + BF, and rejection sampling; 2 for CCC. The paper says higher counts indicate more robustness.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: Unless otherwise specified, evaluations use temperature 0 (greedy). Majority-voting visualizations use temperature 1 and 64 evaluations per sample; rejection sampling uses temperature 1.

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.eval_protocol: Official train/validation/test setup; training examples for exemplar selection, validation for prompt tuning, and test for evaluation. 8-shot prompt; 1,319 test examples. Correct if prediction and gold answer, converted to nearest integer, exactly match.

datasets.eval_protocol: Official splits where available; 8-shot prompt and 1,000 test examples. Correct if prediction and gold answer, converted to nearest integer, exactly match.

datasets.eval_protocol: Official splits where available; 8-shot prompt and 2,096 test examples. The authors manually cleaned the test data, including fixing extraction of answers with multiple values; correct if prediction and gold answer, converted to nearest integer, exactly match.

datasets.name: AQuA
datasets.eval_protocol: Official train/validation/test split; 8-shot prompt and 254 test examples. The method first predicts a numerical answer, then prompts the LM to choose the closest answer option.

datasets.name: StrategyQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Open-domain question-only setting. 6-shot prompt; evaluation uses the test set. Boolean answers are scored by exact match after evaluating prediction and gold as Boolean values.

datasets.name: Date Understanding (BIG-Bench)

datasets.eval_protocol: Use 8 exemplars with K∈{2,3}; evaluate on the concatenation of test folds with K from 2 to 10 (1,042 examples reported). Score by exact match between prediction and gold answer strings.

baselines.name: Standard prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a few-shot prompting method with the same underlying LM and decoding strategies; the authors reran baseline results when needed, including on cleaned test sets.

baselines.name: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a few-shot prompting method with the same underlying LM and decoding strategies; the authors reran baseline results when needed, including on cleaned test sets. The same number of exemplars as in Wei et al. (2022) is used for fair comparison.

baselines.name: Least-to-Most (LtM) prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a few-shot prompting method with the same underlying LM and decoding strategies; the authors reran baseline results when needed, including on cleaned test sets.

baselines.fair_comparison: Reimplemented using the paper’s No NL prompt, with code-davinci-002 and greedy decoding.

baselines.name: Program-Aided Language Models (PAL)
baselines.fair_comparison: Reimplemented using the paper’s No NL prompt, with code-davinci-002 and greedy decoding.

metrics.name: Final answer accuracy
metrics.caveat: A correct answer does not establish that the reasoning chain is valid; the model can reach the answer by chance or with incorrect reasoning. The paper also reports human evaluation of reasoning-chain plausibility.

metrics.name: Human-rated reasoning-chain plausibility/correctness
metrics.caveat: Annotators can mark valid chains incorrectly, and some judgments are affected by dataset ambiguity; the authors inspect annotations and report these issues alongside the ratings.

controls.name: No rationale
controls.detail: Remove rationales from the NL comments; tested in the ablation study on GSM8K, Date Understanding, and CLUTRR (not applicable to SayCan).
controls.rules_out: Whether the rationales contribute to the full prompt’s accuracy.

controls.name: No NL but nudge
controls.detail: Remove NL comments except the prompt’s nudge line; tested in the ablation study.
controls.rules_out: Whether NL comments beyond the nudge line contribute to accuracy.

controls.name: No NL
controls.detail: Remove all NL comments from the reasoning chain; tested in the ablation study.
controls.rules_out: Whether the NL-comment component contributes to accuracy.

controls.name: No solver
controls.detail: Do not call the external solver; instead, add an answer field to each exemplar and let the LM predict the answer.
controls.rules_out: Whether the external solver contributes to the full method’s accuracy.

confounds.name: A correct answer may come from an invalid reasoning chain rather than valid reasoning
confounds.detail: Final-answer accuracy could look high even if the generated chain contains incorrect reasoning or arrives at the answer by chance; the authors specifically note this risk for Boolean StrategyQA answers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human evaluation of reasoning chains that produced correct answers, with annotators labeling correctness and whether NL or symbolic-language components were incorrect; the authors also inspect annotation errors and ambiguity.

confounds.name: The generated chain may not reflect the LM’s internal reasoning
confounds.detail: Even if executing the generated symbolic program determines the final answer, the opaque Translation stage may not represent how the LM arrived at that program or answer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors acknowledge that Translation remains opaque and limit their guarantee to the faithfulness of the Problem Solving stage.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: Report greedy decoding at temperature 0.0 and self-consistency decoding at temperature 0.4 with 40 generations; standard prompting with self-consistency is not reported.

evidence_standards.name: Exemplar robustness runs
evidence_standards.detail: For four datasets, randomly sample exemplars and repeat the process five times in addition to the original run; report mean and standard deviation of accuracy.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation study
evidence_standards.detail: Evaluate 100 reasoning chains per domain, with each question rated by at least three annotators; use majority label for analysis and report annotator agreement.

evidence_standards.name: No stated significance threshold
evidence_standards.detail: The paper does not report a statistical significance test or a margin for treating differences as ties.

datasets.name: REVEAL-Eval
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluation uses REVEAL-Eval only; REVEAL-Open is excluded because it contains low-agreement labels. The benchmark has 704 questions, 1,002 generated CoT answers, and 3,360 steps. Questions are sampled from the evaluation sets of StrategyQA, 2-hop MuSiQue, Sports Understanding, and Fermi, evenly across datasets; answers are generated by Flan-PaLM-540B, GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), and Flan-UL2-20B. Verifiers are evaluated at step level (attribution, logic, and step type) and full-CoT level; the paper reports macro-F1. Attribution verifiers receive the supplied Wikipedia evidence, retrieved using two GTR paragraphs and one BM25 paragraph for each attribution step, with CoT steps decontextualized for retrieval.

baselines.name: Flan-UL2-20B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same REVEAL-Eval tasks. For few-shot prompting, predictions are averaged over five randomly ordered 8-shot prompts drawn from 13 demonstrations per sub-task; demonstrations are class-balanced and balanced across source datasets and labels. In CoT-level evaluation, both single-decision and pipeline variants are reported.

baselines.name: Flan-PaLM-540B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same REVEAL-Eval tasks. For few-shot prompting, predictions are averaged over five randomly ordered 8-shot prompts drawn from 13 demonstrations per sub-task; demonstrations are class-balanced and balanced across source datasets and labels. In CoT-level evaluation, both single-decision and pipeline variants are reported.

baselines.name: PaLM-2-L
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same REVEAL-Eval tasks. For few-shot prompting, predictions are averaged over five randomly ordered 8-shot prompts drawn from 13 demonstrations per sub-task; demonstrations are class-balanced and balanced across source datasets and labels. In CoT-level evaluation, both single-decision and pipeline variants are reported.

baselines.name: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same REVEAL-Eval tasks. In CoT-level evaluation, both single-decision and pipeline variants are reported.

baselines.name: t5-xxl-true
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same REVEAL-Eval tasks; the paper does not report shared hyperparameter tuning or another specific fairness adjustment. The classifier was trained on a mixture of NLI datasets.

baselines.name: FacTool
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the REVEAL-Eval attribution task. The paper supplies FacTool with the dataset’s evidence instead of letting it retrieve evidence separately, for compatibility with the attribution labels.

metrics.name: Macro-F1
metrics.caveat: The paper notes unbalanced class distributions and reports macro-F1; per-class F1 results are also provided.

metrics.name: Per-class F1
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside macro-F1; the paper notes unbalanced class distributions.

metrics.name: Krippendorff’s α
metrics.caveat: The paper reports modest inter-annotator agreement: 0.49 for attribution steps and 0.46 for logical steps.

confounds.name: Unsupported attribution labels may reflect retrieval failure rather than incorrect claims
confounds.detail: A verifier’s attribution results could be affected by whether the supplied evidence supports a claim; unsupported claims are not necessarily false, since retrieval may fail to find relevant evidence.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not fully ruled out. The authors qualitatively examined 40 unsupported steps (10 per source dataset): 19 were factually incorrect; among the remaining 21, they identified retrieval, decontextualization, and additional-knowledge issues, and estimated roughly half of unsupported cases stem from imperfect retrieval. They also acknowledge this limitation.

confounds.name: Low-confidence or ambiguous human labels could make verifier performance look poor
confounds.detail: A low score could reflect annotator disagreement about a step rather than verifier error.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors place any CoT with a step for which fewer than three of five annotators agree on a label for attribution or logical correctness in REVEAL-Open, and evaluate only on REVEAL-Eval.

confounds.name: Few-shot prompt variation could account for differences in LM results
confounds.detail: Few-shot evaluation is noisy, so scores could depend on the selected demonstrations or their order.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Average LM predictions over five randomly ordered 8-shot prompts sampled from 13 demonstrations per sub-task.

evidence_standards.name: Five few-shot prompts per LM evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper averages predictions over five randomly ordered 8-shot prompts, sampled from 13 demonstrations per sub-task; demonstration sets are class-balanced and balanced across source datasets and labels.

evidence_standards.name: Five human annotations per question and CoT answer for each task
evidence_standards.detail: For low-agreement cases, a step is designated low-agreement when fewer than three of five annotators agree on any single attribution or logical-correctness label; such CoTs are assigned to REVEAL-Open, and evaluation uses REVEAL-Eval.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: A single accuracy on the fixed GSM8K questions can hide variation across instantiations; the paper reports accuracy distributions across generated sets and compares them with the original-question accuracy.

controls.name: GSM-Symbolic without No-Op statements
controls.detail: The unaugmented GSM-Symbolic questions serve as the reference condition for GSM-NoOp questions with added inconsequential statements.
controls.rules_out: That the GSM-NoOp performance drop is merely due to using generated question variants rather than the added No-Op statements.

confounds.name: Arithmetic difficulty, rather than reasoning, explains performance changes on GSM-Symbolic
confounds.detail: Changed numerical values or expanded ranges could make arithmetic harder and lower accuracy independently of reasoning robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors choose numerical ranges close to GSM8K and report that Appendix A.6 confirms the expanded ranges remain within boundaries where models maintain arithmetic accuracy.

confounds.name: GSM8K performance is inflated by training-data contamination
confounds.detail: Models may have encountered original GSM8K test examples during training, making their original-question scores optimistic without demonstrating general reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper compares original-question accuracy with the distribution across GSM-Symbolic instantiations and notes the pattern is consistent with possible contamination.

confounds.name: GSM-NoOp failures reflect lack of examples showing how to handle No-Op statements
confounds.detail: The performance drop might be due to unfamiliarity with the added statements rather than an inability to ignore irrelevant information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper tests 8 same-question GSM-Symbolic shots (NoOp-Symb) and 8 different-question GSM-NoOp shots containing No-Op statements (NoOp-NoOp); these do not generally recover performance.

confounds.name: More clauses may not correspond exactly to more reasoning steps
confounds.detail: The difficulty comparison changes clause count, but a clause added or removed does not necessarily change the required reasoning steps by exactly one.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors explicitly qualify this limitation and focus on the evolution of the performance distribution.

evidence_standards.name: Empirical performance distributions over 50 generated sets
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports accuracy distributions across the 50 sets and discusses variance and standard deviation; it does not specify seeds, a statistical test, or a numerical margin for declaring a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: 8-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting with greedy decoding
evidence_standards.detail: This is the common decoding and prompting setup for reported evaluations unless stated otherwise; the paper says preliminary experiments found that changing the number of shots did not significantly change performance or conclusions.

confounds.name: The student may use question-answer correlations and ignore its rationale
confounds.detail: The student could produce a rationale while predicting from a shortcut based on the question, so rationale generation would not explain its answer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure student faithfulness with LAS and test sensitivity by perturbing generated rationales and measuring the change in accuracy.

confounds.name: The negation result reflects overall performance rather than structured handling of negation

confounds.name: The relevance-scoring benefit is confined to questions with smaller retrieved graphs
confounds.detail: A headline gain could arise from performance on questions with fewer entities and smaller, less noisy retrieved KGs rather than helping when the KG is larger.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare accuracy for questions with ≤10 versus >10 entities, with and without the relevance score; the paper reports the two-group results and finds the score especially helps the >10-entity group.

confounds.name: Leaderboard differences reflect other systems’ greater scale or training data, not the method

confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors acknowledge this difference when contextualizing the leaderboard comparisons.

metrics.name: Pass@1
metrics.caveat: A correct final numerical answer does not establish rigorous reasoning; the paper notes that heuristic guesses can produce correct answers. It uses formal proof evaluation as a complementary process-level assessment.

metrics.name: Pass@k
metrics.caveat: The paper says Pass@k is a more comprehensive probe of reasoning capability than Pass@1; it reports it alongside consensus accuracy to show that finding a solution among samples does not imply reliable performance.

metrics.name: Cons@k
metrics.caveat: The gap between Pass@64 and Cons@64 can reveal inconsistency: models may solve a problem in some samples but fail to do so reliably.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Rule-based numerical-answer accuracy checks final answers, not reasoning quality; heuristic shortcuts can create an illusory improvement. The paper also evaluates formal proofs for process-level verification.

metrics.name: n-gram accuracy
metrics.caveat: The normalized difference δ depends on the rewriting LLM, so the paper says leakage risk should be assessed by comparing δ relatively between benchmarks, not by interpreting its absolute value.

confounds.name: Benchmark results may reflect data contamination rather than model capability
confounds.detail: Prior exposure to problems or answers could make performance appear stronger without demonstrating mathematical reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Problems were manually sourced from printed publications; the paper also measures n-gram accuracy by comparing original samples with three LLM-rewritten versions and reports lower relative δ for OlymMATH than PolyMath.

confounds.name: Correct numerical answers may come from heuristic guessing rather than rigorous reasoning
confounds.detail: A model can obtain the headline answer score through shortcuts such as assuming symmetry without proving optimality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses OlymMATH-LEAN, where a proof must compile and prove the theorem, and provides qualitative case studies of guessing. It explicitly concedes that it does not quantify the proportion of guesses in natural-language evaluation.

confounds.name: The English–Chinese performance gap may partly reflect response-extraction failures rather than reasoning ability
confounds.detail: Incorrect Chinese responses could be scored as failures because of language-specific presentation or extraction issues.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Trajectory analysis measures extraction failures and finds them disproportionately frequent among incorrect Chinese responses, identifying a presentation issue distinct from reasoning errors.

evidence_standards.name: Natural-language sampling and scoring
evidence_standards.detail: Generate 64 responses per problem, except the listed resource-intensive models, which use 8. Pass@1 is mean accuracy across sampled responses; Cons@k uses majority voting. Locally evaluated models use temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, min_p 0, max_tokens 32768; API-evaluated models use maximum available max_tokens.

evidence_standards.name: Formal-proof sampling and scoring
evidence_standards.detail: Generate 32 proof attempts per OlymMATH-LEAN problem and report Pass@k; success requires a correct theorem proof that compiles in Lean 4. Use temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 32768.

evidence_standards.name: Cross-language significance test
evidence_standards.detail: Apply Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to released trajectories from 14 models (1.5B, 7B, and 14B) to test EN–ZH differences across subjects and difficulty levels. The paper reports statistical significance but does not state a p-value threshold or confidence intervals.

datasets.name: LILA-TEST
datasets.eval_protocol: For each task, randomly split examples into 70% train, 10% development, and 20% test. Score answer predictions against gold answers with F1; for program synthesis, execute the generated program and score its output against the gold program's output with F1.

datasets.name: LILA-OOD
datasets.eval_protocol: For tasks with multiple datasets, randomly assign datasets to IID and OOD sets; train on the IID set and evaluate generalization on the OOD set from different datasets requiring the same underlying skill. Tasks with only one dataset have no OOD split. Use the paper's F1 scoring for answers or executed program outputs.

datasets.name: LILA-ROBUST
datasets.eval_protocol: Apply linguistic perturbation templates to questions; sample 20 questions from each constituent dataset and obtain perturbed-question annotations via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Evaluate using the paper's F1 scoring for answers or executed program outputs.

Scores use 100 uniformly distributed examples due to cost and usage limits.

metrics.name: F1 score
metrics.caveat: The authors say F1 likely overestimates performance: for the gold answer “2 apples,” predictions “2” and “apples” receive the same score even though “2” is better. They use F1 for lack of a better alternative; for program synthesis they score the executed output rather than the program itself.

controls.name: Single-task GPT-Neo models

controls.rules_out: A multi-task model's gains being explained simply by using the GPT-Neo-2.7B model family or fine-tuning, rather than by training across tasks.

confounds.name: Performance reflects dataset-specific patterns rather than learned mathematical reasoning skills
confounds.detail: A model could score well on the standard test set without generalizing the underlying reasoning skill to independently collected data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on LILA-OOD datasets assigned separately from the IID datasets but requiring the same underlying skills.

confounds.name: Performance depends on the original linguistic phrasing of questions
confounds.detail: A model could succeed on standard questions by relying on familiar surface wording rather than being robust to alternate phrasings.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on LILA-ROBUST questions with linguistic perturbations; the paper reports no performance degradation on perturbed IID test examples for its multi-task model.

datasets.name: Mathador-LM
datasets.eval_protocol: Each model evaluation uses a newly generated problem set. The five operands are sampled uniformly from [1,4], [1,6], [1,8], [1,12], and [1,20]; reachable targets are sampled according to the desired difficulty distribution. Responses are parsed and scored using the Mathador points system: 5 points for reaching the target, points for operators (addition 1, multiplication 1, subtraction 2, division 3), and a 6-point Mathador bonus; invalid solutions score 0. Accuracy is the solution score normalized by the optimal score. The paper does not specify a train/test split or a single fixed evaluation-set size.

metrics.name: Macro-averaged AUROC (overline{AUROC})
metrics.caveat: Pooled AUROC can conflate within-problem discrimination with cross-problem score–difficulty correlation; the paper instead reports macro-averaged AUROC over problems with at least one correct and one wrong initial sample.

metrics.name: Discrimination gap D = r_C − r_W
metrics.caveat: A large D alone does not ensure a large voting advantage when Pass@1 is already close to the Standard MV plateau; the paper considers the gap from Pass@1 to that plateau alongside D.

metrics.name: Token-efficiency ratio B_method/B_MV
metrics.caveat: A ratio is evaluated at a target interpolated between Pass@1 and the Standard MV plateau; the paper reports results at α=75%, 90%, and 99%.

controls.name: Standard MV (unweighted voting)
controls.detail: Aggregates the sampled answers without prefix-consistency weights, and is run alongside PC-WMV under the common token-budget evaluation.
controls.rules_out: That the reported advantage is merely from aggregating multiple samples rather than from the prefix-consistency weighting.

confounds.name: Pooled AUROC could reflect cross-problem score–difficulty correlation rather than within-problem correctness discrimination
confounds.detail: A pooled score can appear discriminative because scores correlate with problem difficulty across problems, even if it does not distinguish correct from wrong traces within a problem.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report macro-averaged AUROC over problems with both correct and wrong initial samples; the paper argues this matches the within-problem comparisons used at vote time.

confounds.name: Token accounting may favor log-probability-based baselines
confounds.detail: The paper treats log-probability access as free, which favors baselines that use log-probabilities without generating extra tokens, while prefix consistency incurs regeneration tokens.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not fully ruled out: the paper acknowledges the accounting is implementation-dependent and says charging for log-probability retrieval would widen the margin; it does not report a measurement with that charge imposed.

confounds.name: Small gains may reflect limited headroom above Pass@1 rather than a strong reweighting advantage
confounds.detail: When Pass@1 is already close to the Standard MV plateau, there is little room for any reweighting method to improve accuracy, irrespective of D.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Pass@1 with the Standard MV plateau and interpret D alongside that headroom; the paper identifies the cells with little PC advantage as those with a small Pass@1-to-plateau gap.

evidence_standards.name: Uncertainty reported as ±2σ confidence intervals

evidence_standards.name: Cluster-bootstrap significance for GLM slopes

evidence_standards.name: Token-efficiency uncertainty

baselines.name: Scaling Metric (Muennighoff et al., 2025)
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported alongside ARISE on the same evaluated models and benchmarks; further comparison controls are not specified.

metrics.name: Scaling Metric
metrics.caveat: Uses aggregate accuracy and can miss sample-level transitions and negative scaling; under performance degradation it can assign higher scores to models that use more tokens for worse results. The paper reports ARISE alongside it.

controls.name: Naive multiple sampling under a fixed budget
controls.detail: Uniformly distributes the same total sampling budget across instances, in comparison with variance-proportional adaptive sampling.
controls.rules_out: That adaptive sampling’s stability improvement is merely due to using a larger total sampling budget.

controls.name: Single-sampling condition
controls.detail: Evaluates the metrics with single sampling, alongside adaptive-sampling conditions.
controls.rules_out: That the reported stability is present without the adaptive-sampling procedure.

controls.name: Artificial negative-scaling perturbation
controls.detail: On original GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.1 AIME trajectories, flips 5–25% of samples that were correct at one scaling level to incorrect at the next.
controls.rules_out: That the metric is insensitive to injected performance degradation.

controls.name: Gaussian token-count-noise perturbation
controls.detail: Adds Gaussian noise to token counts without changing accuracy, with noise magnitude from 0 to 0.3 times the mean token count.
controls.rules_out: That metric behavior under token-count noise is being mistaken for sensitivity to genuine accuracy degradation.

confounds.name: Observed evaluation variability is due to stochastic accuracy and token consumption across trials
confounds.detail: If trial-to-trial variability drives the score, model comparisons may be unstable rather than reflecting scaling behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Adaptive sampling monitors the combined coefficient of variation in accuracy and token consumption and collects samples until the threshold is met or m_max is reached; the paper also reports stability across five independent runs.

confounds.name: ARISE’s response to apparent negative scaling reflects token-count measurement noise rather than genuine degradation
confounds.detail: Token-count noise could change the score even when accuracy and scaling quality are unchanged.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper injects Gaussian token-count noise without changing accuracy and reports ARISE’s coefficient of variation remains below 0.13 at 30% noise.

confounds.name: A metric’s apparent sensitivity to scaling quality does not reflect its response to actual accuracy regressions
confounds.detail: A metric could change little when samples that were correct become incorrect after scaling.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper injects negative scaling by flipping correctly solved samples to incorrect at the next level and measures the resulting metric change.

evidence_standards.name: Five independent runs; report standard deviations
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports standard deviations across five independent runs for stability analyses and computes coefficients of variation across those runs. It specifies no statistical significance test or no-difference margin.

baselines.name: Bayes_U@N (uniform-prior Bayes)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Bayes_R0@N on the same benchmark and trial budget, against the same Bayes_U@80 gold-standard ranking.

baselines.name: Bayes_U@80 (avg@80 gold-standard ranking)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the common reference ranking for methods evaluated on the same benchmark and full set of 80 trials.

baselines.name: HodgeRank
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark outcomes and trial budget as the other ranking methods.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same benchmark data and low-budget single-trial draws as the other methods.

baselines.name: Nanson’s rule with tie averaging
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same benchmark data and low-budget single-trial draws as the other methods.

baselines.name: Pass@k
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark data; excluded from N=1 comparisons because it requires at least two trials.

metrics.name: Kendall’s τ_b
metrics.caveat: High self-consistency with a method’s own full-trial ranking does not imply agreement with the gold standard; the paper reports both gold-standard agreement and self-consistency.

metrics.name: Greedy–sampling alignment (τ_G-S)
metrics.caveat: Alignment is a diagnostic for whether the greedy prior may help, not a guarantee; the reported trend is based on four benchmarks and is considered alongside the change in gold-standard agreement (Δτ).

metrics.name: Δτ (greedy-prior minus uniform-prior gold-standard agreement)
metrics.caveat: A change in mean agreement alone does not capture the prior’s variance reduction; the paper also reports the relative reduction in the standard deviation of τ_b.

controls.name: Uniform-prior Bayes@N
controls.detail: The empirical-prior Bayes_R0@N condition is compared with Bayes_U@N, which does not incorporate the greedy decode as a prior.
controls.rules_out: Whether the observed change is specifically associated with adding the greedy empirical prior rather than using the uniform-prior estimator.

confounds.name: Greedy decoding and stochastic sampling induce different rankings
confounds.detail: The greedy empirical prior can shrink rankings toward a different ordering, producing bias even while reducing low-budget variance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure greedy–sampling alignment as Kendall’s τ_b between greedy and stochastic-sampling rankings at N=80, and report the change in gold-standard agreement (Δτ) alongside the standard-deviation reduction.

confounds.name: A method can appear stable while being systematically far from correctness-based ranking
confounds.detail: High agreement with a method’s own full-trial ordering may reflect self-consistency rather than accuracy relative to the paper’s gold standard.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report both Kendall’s τ_b against Bayes_U@80 and τ_b against the method’s own full-trial ranking.

confounds.name: Low-budget conclusions depend on which models are in the evaluation pool
confounds.detail: The reported winner or ranking stability could be an artifact of the full 20-model pool.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Repeat the low-budget analysis on bootstrapped pools of 5, 10, and 15 models, aggregating 1,000 subsets for each benchmark–size setting.

confounds.name: Auxiliary categorical signals can stabilize rankings while shifting them away from correctness-based ordering
confounds.detail: Signals such as verifier judgments or OOD robustness may produce strong self-consistency but a biased ordering relative to the gold standard.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For categorical schemes, report both τ_b against Bayes_U@80 and self-consistency against each scheme’s own full-trial ranking; also compare with Bayes_R0@80.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated single-trial draws
evidence_standards.detail: For N=1 analyses, subsample one of the 80 available trials per question, compute rankings, and report mean ± standard deviation of Kendall’s τ_b over 80 draws.

evidence_standards.name: Resampled-dataset uncertainty for prior comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: For the Bayes_R0@N versus Bayes_U@N comparison, report mean and standard deviation over 50 resampled datasets.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrapped model-pool robustness
evidence_standards.detail: Aggregate 1,000 bootstrapped model subsets for each benchmark and pool size (5, 10, and 15), reporting mean and standard deviation across subsets.

evidence_standards.name: Categorical-ranking draw variability
evidence_standards.detail: For the N=1 categorical-ranking experiment, report mean ± standard deviation over 80 draws.

baselines.name: PPO
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper contrasts PPO with GRPO as RL algorithms; it does not specify a matched benchmark comparison protocol in the provided experimental text.

baselines.name: RFT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with online RFT in the training-method experiments; both are described as using SFT questions, with RFT sampling from the SFT model and online RFT sampling from the real-time policy.

baselines.name: Online RFT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with RFT and GRPO in the training-method experiments; the paper identifies online sampling as the distinction from offline RFT.

baselines.name: DPO
baselines.fair_comparison: Included among the training methods analyzed in the unified paradigm; no matched evaluation protocol is specified here.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Table 5 mixes top-1 scores with majority-vote scores from 32 candidates; the paper marks the majority-vote scores separately.

metrics.name: Maj@K
metrics.caveat: The authors note that RL improves Maj@K but not Pass@K, so a higher Maj@K may reflect a more robust output distribution or a higher chance of selecting a correct response among samples rather than stronger fundamental capability; they report Pass@K alongside it.

metrics.name: Pass@K
metrics.caveat: The authors report that RL does not improve Pass@K even when Maj@K improves, and use the two measures together to distinguish sampling-distribution changes from increased underlying capability.

controls.name: General-token training instead of code-token training
controls.detail: For the code-training experiment, the paper compares 400B code tokens followed by 150B math tokens with 400B general tokens followed by the same 150B math tokens.
controls.rules_out: That the gains from the code-then-math condition are merely due to adding a 400B-token first training stage before math training.

controls.name: No math training
controls.detail: The paper reports a no-math-training reference alongside math-corpus and code/math training conditions.
controls.rules_out: That downstream performance in those experiments is simply the model's unmodified, pre-math-training performance.

controls.name: DeepSeekMath-Instruct before RL
controls.detail: DeepSeekMath-RL is evaluated against the starting DeepSeekMath-Instruct model; the RL training uses GSM8K- and MATH-related chain-of-thought questions and excludes other SFT questions to examine benchmarks without data during the RL phase.
controls.rules_out: That reported differences are just the starting instruction-tuned model's scores; the exclusion also supports examination of performance on benchmarks not included in RL training.

controls.name: GRPO with outcome supervision (GRPO+OS)
controls.detail: Compared with GRPO using process supervision (GRPO+PS).
controls.rules_out: A difference favoring GRPO+PS supports the value of fine-grained, step-aware supervision rather than outcome-only supervision.

controls.name: Offline RFT
controls.detail: RFT samples outputs from the initial SFT model, while online RFT samples from the real-time policy; the paper compares their training curves.
controls.rules_out: Whether online sampling, rather than offline sampling from the initial SFT model, accounts for the later-stage gains.

controls.name: Online RFT
controls.detail: Compared with GRPO, which uses reward-model values to adjust positive and negative gradient coefficients; online RFT uniformly reinforces correct responses and does not penalize incorrect ones.
controls.rules_out: Whether GRPO's gains are attributable to differential positive and negative reinforcement rather than online sampling alone.

confounds.name: RL improves sampling robustness rather than fundamental reasoning capability
confounds.detail: The headline benchmark gains could arise because RL makes correct responses more likely to appear among samples or be selected, without improving the model's underlying capability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures Pass@K and Maj@K on GSM8K and MATH at temperature 0.7. It finds that RL improves Maj@K but not Pass@K; this does not rule out the alternative and is presented as evidence consistent with it.

confounds.name: Benchmark contamination in pre-training data
confounds.detail: Benchmark gains could reflect benchmark questions or answers appearing in the Common Crawl-derived math corpus rather than general mathematical learning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors filter web pages containing benchmark text: exact matching of 10-gram strings, and exact matching for benchmark texts shorter than 10 grams but at least 3 grams.

confounds.name: The apparent quality of the DeepSeekMath Corpus is due to greater training-data quantity rather than higher average quality
confounds.detail: A larger corpus could yield stronger results even if its data were not higher quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare learning curves at 50B tokens, described as one full Proof-Pile-2 epoch, and report that the model trained on the DeepSeekMath Corpus performs better at that point.

confounds.name: RL gains on evaluation benchmarks come from training on those benchmarks' questions
confounds.detail: Improvements could result from direct exposure to evaluation questions during RL rather than the RL method's effects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The RL training uses GSM8K- and MATH-related SFT questions and excludes other SFT questions; the paper identifies the other benchmarks as out-of-domain for this RL phase. GSM8K and MATH themselves remain in-domain.

confounds.name: ArXiv math text should improve mathematical reasoning, but the observed comparison may depend on task coverage or scale
confounds.detail: The authors explicitly caution that their negative result for arXiv training may not extend to untested math-related tasks, mixtures with other data, or larger models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper reports experiments on the included reasoning and formal-mathematics benchmarks, but explicitly leaves those task, mixture, and scale limitations for future work.

evidence_standards.name: Reported evaluation prompting and decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports few-shot chain-of-thought prompting for the relevant reasoning evaluations, few-shot program-of-thought prompting for Python-assisted GSM8K and MATH, zero-shot HumanEval, and few-shot MBPP. Figure 7 reports Pass@K and Maj@K at temperature 0.7.

evidence_standards.name: Top-1 versus majority-vote reporting
evidence_standards.detail: In Table 5, scores in gray are majority votes over 32 candidates; other scores are top-1. The paper does not specify seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests in the provided experimental text.

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the train and test splits, randomly selecting 3,000 samples from each (or all if a split has fewer than 3,000). Concatenates question and solution with a space; calculates perplexity on the solution only and 5- and 10-gram accuracy on the combined text. For n-gram accuracy, uniformly samples 5 starting points from positions 2 to the end of the combined text; exact match is the default. Compares each split with three ChatGPT-paraphrased reference versions and averages their metrics. In the meta-experiment, uses 1,000 seen and 1,000 unseen examples.

datasets.name: MATH
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the train and test splits, randomly selecting 3,000 samples from each (or all if a split has fewer than 3,000). Concatenates question and solution with a space; calculates perplexity on the solution only and 5- and 10-gram accuracy on the combined text. For n-gram accuracy, uniformly samples 5 starting points from positions 2 to the end of the combined text; exact match is the default. Compares each split with three ChatGPT-paraphrased reference versions and averages their metrics. In the meta-experiment, uses 1,000 seen and 1,000 unseen examples.

metrics.name: Perplexity (PPL)
metrics.caveat: PPL and n-gram accuracy can give different rankings because PPL is a continuous probability measure while n-gram accuracy requires exact subsequence matches and is sensitive to formatting. The paper reports both; PPL is calculated on the solution portion only.

metrics.name: N-gram Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Exact matching is sensitive to reformatting or paraphrasing and can miss leakage in modified formats. The paper also reports PPL and uses ROUGE-L and edit-distance similarity for looser instance-level comparisons.

metrics.name: ROUGE-L
metrics.caveat: Used as a lenient instance-level match rather than the default exact-match score; the paper also considers edit-distance similarity.

metrics.name: Edit distance similarity
metrics.caveat: Used as a lenient instance-level match rather than the default exact-match score; the paper also considers ROUGE-L.

metrics.name: Decrement (Δ), percentage decrease (δ), and train-test disparity (δ_train-test)
metrics.caveat: A large percentage can be unreliable when the absolute decrement is small; the paper says to consider the absolute Δ alongside the percentages. A near-zero train-test disparity can mean either no leakage or leakage in both splits, so it is not conclusive by itself.

controls.name: Synthesized paraphrase reference benchmarks
controls.detail: For each benchmark, the paper generates three paraphrased reference versions with ChatGPT, measures the same atomic metric on them, and averages the results for comparison with the original benchmark.
controls.rules_out: A difference is evidence of greater familiarity with the original benchmark relative to paraphrases intended to preserve its format and reasoning difficulty; it is not by itself proof of leakage.

controls.name: Untrained Mistral-7B-v0.1 in the meta-experiment
controls.detail: The paper compares benchmark-trained Mistral-7B-v0.1 variants (pre-training or supervised fine-tuning on benchmark data) with the model without benchmark-data training.
controls.rules_out: Whether the observed metric changes accompany benchmark-data training rather than the model’s baseline behavior.

controls.name: Unseen benchmark examples in the meta-experiment
controls.detail: Alongside the 1,000 examples used for training, the paper evaluates on another 1,000 examples the model was not exposed to.
controls.rules_out: Whether metric changes are specific to seen examples rather than reflecting generalization to unseen benchmark examples.

confounds.name: Both train and test splits may be contaminated, making the train-test disparity appear small
confounds.detail: A near-zero δ_train-test can look like no leakage even when both splits were used in training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper supplements the disparity with train- and test-split Δ and δ values and instance-level n-gram predictions. It notes that simultaneous leakage cannot be fully detected by the disparity pipeline.

confounds.name: Benchmark data may have been reformatted or paraphrased during training
confounds.detail: A model exposed to modified benchmark text may fail exact n-gram matches, making n-gram accuracy understate familiarity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also measures PPL and reports lenient instance-level comparisons using ROUGE-L and edit-distance similarity; it notes that n-gram detection remains limited when the original format and wording are not retained.

confounds.name: Model size and capability can affect raw metric decrements
confounds.detail: Differences in raw Δ across models could reflect model scale or capability rather than differing benchmark familiarity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper normalizes the decrement by the original metric score to obtain δ for comparisons across models.

confounds.name: A small absolute decrement can produce a large, unstable percentage
confounds.detail: A large δ_train-test may appear compelling even when it is driven by small absolute changes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says to consider the absolute Δ alongside the percentage, citing Phi-2 as an example.

confounds.name: Synthetic references may introduce phraseology bias or differ from the original benchmark
confounds.detail: A metric difference could arise from differences introduced by synthesis rather than benchmark familiarity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper aims to preserve format and reasoning difficulty through paraphrasing and averages results across three synthesized versions to mitigate synthesis randomness; it acknowledges phraseology bias as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding for n-gram predictions
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states that all models use greedy decoding by default.

evidence_standards.name: Average across three synthesized reference versions
evidence_standards.detail: The paper generates three reference versions per benchmark and averages their metrics to mitigate randomness from synthesis; generation uses temperature 0.7 and top_p 0.9.

evidence_standards.name: Train-test disparity as a qualitative leakage heuristic
evidence_standards.detail: A significant δ_train-test is interpreted as potential disproportionate familiarity with one split; a near-zero value is ambiguous between no leakage and simultaneous leakage. The paper specifies no statistical test, confidence interval, seed-based variance rule, or numerical significance threshold.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: For GPT-4 on Coin Flip, accuracy is already 100%, so the paper says there is no need to run SC or ESC; accuracy is reported alongside ESC's average actual sample count.

metrics.name: Average actual number of generated samples (L̂)
metrics.caveat: Does not by itself indicate whether performance is maintained; the paper reports accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: L1 norm
metrics.caveat: Used to measure consistency between predicted and actual sampling cost and performance change; reported alongside Pearson correlation.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: Used to measure consistency between predicted and actual sampling cost and performance change; reported alongside L1 norm, with p-values.

metrics.name: Performance change percentage between SC and ESC (Pδ)
metrics.caveat: The paper evaluates how well the control scheme predicts this quantity by comparing predicted and actual values, using L1 norm and Pearson correlation.

metrics.name: Intersection ratio between ESC and SC voting results
metrics.caveat: Measures agreement of voting results rather than accuracy; the paper uses it to support the reliability of its bound on performance impact.

controls.name: SC with sample size matched to ESC's average actual sample count (L̂-SC)

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: A single response order can be affected by positional bias; the paper evaluates each pair again with the order swapped and aggregates the two judgments. Ties in both trials and inconsistent decisions count as incorrect.

controls.name: Claude-3.5-Sonnet-generated response pairs
controls.detail: The authors regenerate pairs with Claude-3.5-Sonnet rather than GPT-4o, yielding 270 pairs, and compare model performance across the two pair-generation conditions.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether results depend specifically on GPT-4o generating the pairs; the comparison shows generation-model bias is present and quantifies it, rather than eliminating it.

confounds.name: Pair-generation-model bias
confounds.detail: Because GPT-4o generates the response pairs, the benchmark may be disproportionately difficult for GPT-4o judges, and the generated questions may not be equally challenging for other models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Regenerate pairs with Claude-3.5-Sonnet and compare model performance. The authors report the change in performance for both generators and say other models show similar performance gaps.

confounds.name: Positional bias
confounds.detail: A judge’s choice may depend on which response is presented first, making a single-order accuracy score misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run the judge twice with the response order swapped and aggregate the decisions; inconsistent choices and ties in both trials count as incorrect.

confounds.name: Formatting artifacts in automated correctness checks
confounds.detail: A correct response can be marked incorrect because of a formatting mismatch, giving judges an unintended shortcut rather than testing correctness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use GPT-4o-mini to extract and assess the solution independently, filter responses where it disagrees with the automated checker, and manually inspect disagreements.

confounds.name: Stylistic differences or self-enhancement bias
confounds.detail: If responses come from different models, judges might rely on writing style or favor responses from their own model instead of assessing correctness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Generate all candidate responses for the main benchmark with one model to keep response style consistent and mitigate self-enhancement bias.

evidence_standards.name: Two judgments per response pair with swapped order
evidence_standards.detail: The paper aggregates the two judgments: a consistent preference for the correct response, or that preference paired with a tie, is counted correct; inconsistent choices and ties in both trials are counted incorrect. No seeds, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or explicit threshold for declaring a difference real are reported.

metrics.name: Accuracy (ACC) / pass@1
metrics.caveat: Standard accuracy treats solving an easy problem as equivalent to solving a top-level problem; the paper also reports difficulty-weighted accuracy (DW-ACC). Answers are checked with rule-based matching, reported to have over 98% precision in sampled human inspection.

controls.name: Uncontrolled-output reference condition
controls.detail: The ordinary evaluation prompt asks for the final answer in a box and adds no language-control instruction; it is compared with prompts forcing the query language, forcing English, or allowing the model to choose a preferred language.
controls.rules_out: Provides a no-language-control reference for assessing whether the language-control prompt conditions change performance; it does not isolate the effect of adding an instruction from the effect of its language constraint.

confounds.name: Observed cross-language gaps could be sampling variability
confounds.detail: Language accuracy differences might reflect run-to-run variation rather than genuine language differences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test each model 16 times with fixed hyperparameters, report average@16 and standard deviations, and compare the observed gaps with reported run fluctuations of about 0.5–1.5% ACC.

confounds.name: Apparent language-control effects could reflect failure to follow the requested output language
confounds.detail: Performance differences across language-control prompts might arise because models do not actually comply with the requested language, rather than from the effect of reasoning in that language.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Analyze instruction-following degree under language control by measuring whether outputs adhere to the requested language (details in Appendix F.2).

confounds.name: Translation errors or fluency problems could create apparent language performance gaps
confounds.detail: A translated problem with altered content or unclear wording could change model accuracy independently of multilingual reasoning ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use expert translation calibration and report annotator content- and fluency-disagreement rates for GPT-4o pre-translations. The paper also concedes that fully idiomatic expression cannot be guaranteed for all languages.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated runs and variance
evidence_standards.detail: Each model is tested 16 times under fixed hyperparameters; results are reported as average@16, with standard-deviation analyses. The paper says multi-run ACC fluctuations are mostly about 0.5–1.5%; it reports no formal statistical test or explicit significance threshold.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding and output limit
evidence_standards.detail: Non-reasoning open-source models use greedy decoding. Open-source reasoning models use sampling with T=0.6, p=0.95, k=20. The maximum output limit is 65,536 tokens, or the model's stricter limit.

evidence_standards.name: Answer verification
evidence_standards.detail: A rule-based answer-matching script is used; sampled human inspection is reported to show over 98% precision.

metrics.caveat: Measures local pairwise inconsistency, not global logical coherence; reported alongside TOV.

controls.name: Judgments with answer order reversed
controls.detail: For every unordered answer pair, the judge evaluates both the forward and reversed presentation orders.
controls.rules_out: A preference reversal attributable only to one presentation order; the paired judgments also allow the paper to measure positional inconsistency.

controls.name: Rubric-free judging
controls.detail: Compared with a condition where the judge generates a rubric once per question and uses it as a fixed standard for all answer pairs.
controls.rules_out: That the consistency improvement from rubric-guided judging occurs without the fixed-rubric intervention.

controls.name: Direct verdict without rationale
controls.detail: A modified prompt tells judges to give the decision directly, without an explanation; compared with the main prompt that requests detailed reasoning.
controls.rules_out: That the reported effect of explicit reasoning is independent of asking the judge to provide a rationale.

controls.name: Unmodified base judge models
controls.detail: Fine-tuned judges are compared with their corresponding base models on Sage.
controls.rules_out: That the fine-tuning result is merely the performance of the underlying base checkpoint.

controls.name: POLL aggregate versus best individual panel member
controls.detail: For each panel, compare the aggregated judgment with the best individual model in that panel.
controls.rules_out: That panel aggregation’s improvement is just the performance of its strongest individual member.

controls.name: Alternative ChatEval configurations
controls.detail: The paper varies rounds, judge selection, and argument-exchange format and compares these settings with the non-debate baseline.
controls.rules_out: That ChatEval’s reported degradation is specific to the original configuration.

controls.name: Sage-Hard with Qwen3-235B-A22B-generated answers
controls.detail: The answer generator is changed from Gemini-2.5-Flash to Qwen3-235B-A22B and judge consistency is re-evaluated.
controls.rules_out: That Sage-Hard’s difficulty is an artifact of Gemini-2.5-Flash’s particular writing patterns.

controls.name: Different temperature settings
controls.detail: The paper evaluates model consistency across various temperature settings and reports that the scores remain consistent.
controls.rules_out: That the reported consistency results are merely artifacts of a particular temperature setting.

confounds.name: Stochastic sampling variation in judge outputs
confounds.detail: Metric variation could reflect transient randomness rather than stable judge behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: IPI and TOV are measured across 10 independent runs for two Qwen models, and the paper reports low observed variances; it also gives theoretical aggregate variance bounds.

confounds.name: Temperature-dependent sampling artifacts
confounds.detail: The consistency results could depend on the chosen temperature rather than the judge’s underlying behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluate consistency across various temperatures and report small variance and consistent IPI and TOV scores.

confounds.name: Sage-Hard difficulty is specific to Gemini-2.5-Flash answer style
confounds.detail: High inconsistency could come from the source model’s generation patterns rather than the challenge of distinguishing similarly capable answers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They replace Gemini-2.5-Flash with Qwen3-235B-A22B as answer generator and report only small IPI and TOV changes.

confounds.name: Judges lack the ability to make just judgments, rather than applying shifting criteria across answer pairs
confounds.detail: The observed inconsistency might reflect inability to judge correctly, not situational preferences that change with the compared answers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A rubric generated once per question and fixed across pairs reduces IPI and TOV, which the authors interpret as evidence that explicit criteria mitigate situational preferences.

confounds.name: Human consistency scores are inflated by memory or context priming
confounds.detail: Annotators might remember their earlier judgment of a pair or be primed by consecutive pairs from the same question.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Forward and reversed versions of a pair go to different annotators, and pairs from the same question are interleaved with other questions.

evidence_standards.name: Independent-run variance check
evidence_standards.detail: Two representative Qwen judges are evaluated in 10 independent runs; the paper reports variance for IPI and TOV, without specifying a significance test or a threshold for calling a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: Default-temperature reporting for the main benchmark
evidence_standards.detail: The 13-model benchmark is conducted at default temperature for a fair and consistent comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Temperature sensitivity check
evidence_standards.detail: The paper evaluates performance across various temperatures and reports small variance and remarkable score consistency; no specific temperature values are given in the supplied text.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation study size and assignment
evidence_standards.detail: 20 graduate-level students evaluate a sampled 50 questions from Sage-Easy and Sage-Hard; reversed versions of a pair are assigned to different annotators, and same-question pairs are interleaved.

evidence_standards.name: Correlation significance reporting
evidence_standards.detail: For the Spearman correlations in the external-benchmark validation, the paper reports p-values below 0.001.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy alone can obscure whether an apparent gain reflects improved capability or a higher answer rate accompanied by more errors; the paper recommends reporting hallucination rate and abstention rate alongside it.

metrics.name: Hallucination ratio
metrics.caveat: Because changes can reflect willingness to answer or abstain rather than improved factual recall, report accuracy and abstention behavior alongside it.

confounds.name: Hallucination changes reflect willingness to answer or abstain, not changes in factual knowledge
confounds.detail: A lower hallucination ratio could come from abstaining instead of answering correctly; a higher ratio could come from attempting questions previously left unanswered, rather than worsening knowledge.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For questions whose hallucination outcome changed between reasoning levels, the paper labels responses correct, incorrect, or not attempted, and measures whether non-hallucinating responses are correct or abstentions and whether new hallucinations came from previously unattempted questions.

confounds.name: Automatic grading errors explain the reported results
confounds.detail: If the automatic grader often mislabels answers, the reported accuracy and hallucination patterns could be grading artifacts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors compared automatic grading with human annotations on a random sample of 300 cases and found 2 disagreements.

evidence_standards.name: Trend thresholds for accuracy and hallucination
evidence_standards.detail: The summary labels accuracy as consistently improving only with gains greater than 2% across consecutive reasoning levels. It labels hallucination as consistently decreasing or increasing only with a change greater than 2%; otherwise patterns are marked inconsistent or fluctuating.

evidence_standards.name: Human validation of automatic grading
evidence_standards.detail: The authors randomly sampled 300 cases for comparison with human annotations and report 2 disagreements.

datasets.name: V-STaR
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 14 Video-LLMs on 2,094 videos using both RSTR chains, “what-when-where” and “what-where-when”; no train/test split is specified. Frames are sampled at 1 fps, with uniform sampling up to the model’s maximum allowed frames when a video exceeds its input limit. Videos are also analyzed by duration: short [0,1] min, medium (1,3] min, and long (3,60] min. “What” answers are scored by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct from 0–4; scores above 2 count as correct. The benchmark is built from annotated sources including VidSTG, TVQA+, and GOT-10K, plus YouTube videos; samples that are too short or have too large a moment-to-video-length ratio are filtered out.

metrics.name: Accuracy (Acc)

metrics.caveat: Scoring each question in isolation ignores connections between answers in the reasoning chain; the paper also reports AM and LGM.

metrics.caveat: Scoring each question in isolation ignores connections between answers in the reasoning chain; the paper also reports AM and LGM.

metrics.name: Arithmetic Mean (AM), mean AM (mAM)
metrics.caveat: AM is susceptible to extreme values; the paper also reports LGM. mAM averages AM across the different chains.

metrics.name: Logarithmic Geometric Mean (LGM), mean LGM (mLGM)
metrics.caveat: The ordinary geometric mean becomes zero if any component metric is zero; LGM is introduced to avoid that and to reflect the contribution of the remaining metrics. The paper reports AM alongside it.

confounds.name: Correct answers may come from pretrained co-occurrence biases rather than video-specific spatio-temporal reasoning
confounds.detail: A model could answer the “what” question correctly from prior co-occurrence knowledge without using the video’s temporal or spatial evidence.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The benchmark also measures temporal grounding (R1@tIoU thresholds and m_tIoU), spatial grounding (AP@vIoU thresholds and m_vIoU), and joint performance using temporal and spatial thresholds.

confounds.name: Poor later-chain performance may result from errors propagated from earlier steps rather than failure on the later reasoning component itself
confounds.detail: An incorrect earlier answer could contaminate the information supplied to a subsequent question and lower its score.
confounds.ruled_out_by: In each chain, subsequent questions include the ground truth of earlier questions, allowing temporal and spatial reasoning to be evaluated without propagating earlier model errors.

confounds.name: The order of the reasoning chain may change results for the same questions
confounds.detail: The same questions can yield different results depending on whether the chain is “what-when-where” or “what-where-when.”
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates both chain orders and reports mean AM and mean LGM across chains.
